title: Quantised charge and charge transfer

learning_outcomes.text: understand that the charge on charge carriers is quantised

external_knowledge: The ampere, A, is the SI base unit of electric current.

prior_knowledge_summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge.
A current is produced when mobile charge carriers cross a section.
Electrons are charge carriers in metals and ions are charge carriers in electrolytes.
new_learning: Charge transfer can be found from current and time, and particle counts must be whole-number multiples of elementary charge.

blocks.heading: Can an isolated object have any charge at all?
content: Suppose a tiny oil drop has charge +5.6 × 10^-19 C. Could that charge exist on an isolated object, or must nature build charge in fixed steps?
The puzzle needs two ideas: a smallest charge step and a way to connect a measured current with the charge that has moved.

figure.purpose: Create the need for discrete charge steps.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a row of identical charge tokens labelled e building allowed totals e, 2e, 3e and 4e, beside one questioned total of 3.5e. Do not reveal whether the questioned total is allowed.
figure.alt_text: Identical elementary-charge tokens build whole-number totals beside a questioned fractional total.

blocks.heading: Charge comes in elementary steps
content: Definition to learn: charge exists only in discrete amounts that are integer multiples of the elementary charge.

This is called charge quantisation. The magnitude of the elementary charge is e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C. An electron has charge -e and a proton has charge +e. The sign tells the type of charge; the integer multiple tells how many elementary charges make the total.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: charge exists only in discrete amounts that are integer multiples of the elementary charge

figure.purpose: Distinguish sign from the whole-number size of charge.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw electron and proton symbols beside -e and +e, then a number line with allowed isolated charges at integer multiples of e. Avoid field or force arrows.
figure.alt_text: A charge number line marks positive and negative integer multiples of elementary charge.

blocks.heading: Count elementary charges with Q = Ne
content: Q is total charge in coulombs, C. N is the number of elementary charges and has no unit. e is 1.60 × 10^-19 C. For an isolated object's charge, N must be a whole number.
To test a proposed charge, calculate N = |Q|/e. A whole-number result is allowed by quantisation. A non-integer result is not.

figure.purpose: Teach the whole-number test for quantisation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a worked decision path: take magnitude of Q, divide by e, inspect whether N is an integer. Include +6.40 × 10^-19 C giving N = 4 and +5.60 × 10^-19 C giving N = 3.5.
figure.alt_text: A decision path tests two charges by dividing their magnitudes by elementary charge.

blocks.heading: Connect current, charge and time
content: Q is charge transferred in coulombs, C. I is current in amperes, A. t is time in seconds, s. Convert minutes or milliseconds before substituting.
A current of 0.30 A for 40 s transfers Q = It = 0.30 × 40 = 12 C. Check the meaning: 0.30 A is 0.30 C passing each second, so 40 equal seconds transfer 12 C.

figure.purpose: Connect the rate meaning of current to accumulated charge over time.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a wire cross-section and a time strip of 40 one-second intervals grouped into blocks. Annotate 0.30 C each second and total 12 C, with Q = It below.
figure.alt_text: A wire cross-section and time strip show charge accumulating at a constant rate for 40 seconds.

blocks.heading: From current to a number of electrons
content: A metal wire carries 0.12 A for 80 s. First find the transferred charge: Q = It = 0.12 × 80 = 9.6 C.
Now count the elementary charges: N = Q/e = 9.6/(1.60 × 10^-19) = 6.0 × 10^19 electrons.
Carry the intermediate value with its unit. Independent check: 6.0 × 10^19 × 1.60 × 10^-19 C = 9.6 C, which returns the transferred charge.

figure.purpose: Teach a complete two-stage calculation with a reverse check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use an annotated worked layout with stage 1 Q = It, a boxed carry value 9.6 C, stage 2 N = Q/e, and a reverse multiplication check. Keep signs and powers of ten aligned.
figure.alt_text: A two-stage worked layout finds charge and then electron count, followed by a reverse check.

blocks.heading: Quantised does not mean the current must jump visibly
content: It is tempting to think that quantised charge makes every ordinary current visibly jerky. One electron is an extremely small charge, and enormous numbers of carriers cross a wire section in everyday times.

The total still consists of integer elementary steps, but those steps are too small to notice on an ordinary ammeter. Treating charge flow as smooth on a large scale does not remove its particle structure.

figure.purpose: Reconcile discrete microscopic charge with apparently smooth macroscopic current.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Compare a magnified staircase of individual e steps with a zoomed-out line that appears smooth. Label microscopic view and ordinary scale only.
figure.alt_text: A microscopic charge staircase appears smooth when viewed at an ordinary scale.

blocks.heading: Choose the route before calculating
content: If current and time are given, start with Q = It. If total charge and carrier count are connected, use Q = Ne. If both stages are needed, calculate Q first, carry it in coulombs, then calculate N.
For a quantisation test, N must be an integer. For a number of transferred carriers, a very large scientific-notation answer is normal.
Keep the Lesson 1 model in view: Q = It describes how much charge the moving carriers transfer. It does not yet explain their microscopic drift speed; that comes next.

figure.purpose: Summarise formula selection and the boundary to Lesson 3.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Create a flow chart with given I and t leading to Q = It, then optional Q and e leading to N = Q/e; a separate branch tests whether N is an integer. End before any drift-speed equation.
figure.alt_text: A formula-selection flow chart links current and time to charge and then to carrier count.

evidence_basis.evidence_scope_note: Mapped mixed questions are reduced to their charge-quantisation and charge-transfer leaves; electric-field methods are excluded.

concepts_taught: charge quantisation in integer elementary-charge steps
charge transferred by a steady current over time
misconceptions_addressed: Any fractional multiple of e can be the net charge on an isolated object.
Quantised charge makes ordinary current visibly discontinuous.
Minutes may be substituted directly into Q = It when current is in amperes.
next_lesson_can_assume: Charge exists in integer multiples of e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C.
Use of Q = Ne and the whole-number quantisation test.
Use of Q = It with time in seconds.
A two-stage route can connect current and time to carrier number.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Potential difference, resistance or circuit-network methods.
